name: The Anthropic–Pentagon split
frame: The Department of Defense moving its classified AI work off Anthropic after a dispute over surveillance and autonomous-weapons contract terms.
question: Does the transition complete on schedule, and what replaces the contract safeguards Anthropic sought? Settled by: a department statement or filing after 30 September confirming completion, or a court order pausing it.

text: As of 14 September the transition is nearly done, on one official's word. Emil Michael, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, told DefenseScoop that about 90% of classified AI workloads have moved off Anthropic, with the rest due by the end of September; DefenseScoop reports OpenAI's ChatGPT, xAI's Grok and Google's Gemini are being deployed in its place, and that the break followed Anthropic's attempt to secure contract terms preventing use for mass surveillance of US citizens or fully autonomous lethal weapons, which the department rejected. No other outlet had matched the figure as of this snapshot, and no contract documents have been published.

As of 28 September the split has a published court judgment and the Department's reasons are on the record in the government's own words. The D.C. Circuit decided Anthropic PBC v. United States Department of War in late September. Circuit Judge Katsas wrote for the court, Circuit Judge Henderson dissented, and CNBC and Courthouse News both report the vote as 2-1 with Circuit Judge Rao joining. The opinion states that the Department excluded Claude from its supply chain under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act after Anthropic refused to relax contractual prohibitions on the use of Claude for lethal autonomous warfare or domestic surveillance, and that the Department had ample support for its conclusion that continued integration of Claude presented a statutorily covered national-security risk. It records that Under Secretary for Research and Engineering Emil Michael cited Anthropic's refusal to allow all lawful uses and its ability to alter system guardrails and model weights. Anthropic's due-process and First Amendment claims were rejected.

What the ruling does not settle is the thing this storyline tracks. The opinion never mentions GenAI.mil, the Maven Smart System, or any model that replaced Claude; the transition status rests where it did, on one official's word. Henderson's dissent argues the case turns entirely on the scope of the residual clause and warns that a future contractor faces a choice between agreeing to the Secretary's demands or being designated a national security threat. An Anthropic spokesperson said the company is considering all options, including further review, and noted that another federal court has held a parallel designation unlawful; Breaking Defense reports the remaining routes are a discretionary en banc rehearing or a Supreme Court petition. No department statement or filing confirming completion of the transition has been published.
states.changed: The dispute moved from a procurement decision to a precedent: a federal appeals court upheld the exclusion and put the Department's reasoning into a published opinion, with a dissent arguing the ruling lets the Secretary condition supplier status on dropping use restrictions. The transition itself is still unconfirmed by any department statement or filing.

text: As of 12 October the department has said in words what no document has yet recorded. A Department of Defense official said in a statement in the first week of October that the Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the BBC reported — the first time the department has said the transition is done. The BBC adds that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, set a six-month phase-out at the end of that month and announced the Pentagon would stop using it by late August, and that "It is not clear why there has been a delay." No filing, memorandum or published department document records the completion, and the statement names no replacement. The BBC is the only outlet carrying it.

What the record does contain is the other side's account. On CBS's "Face the Nation", Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar said "there's been no operational impact from that", that the Department "has a wide range of model providers, everything from XAI and OpenAI to open-weight models like Nemotron from NVIDIA", and "It's already been replaced. It's already been replaced." He named no provider for any specific role and gave no figures for the volume of work moved, and the Department has not confirmed his assessment. Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that Claude was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran as recently as the week before the statement, and that the Pentagon has signed contracts with Google, xAI and OpenAI.

On the safeguards this question also tracks, the supplier moved and the government did not. Anthropic published a Usage Policy update, effective November 12, stating that "The updated section makes clear that our prohibitions include the software and components that make weapons work, as well as actions like arming drones and other autonomous vehicles", and that "Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process. We also prohibit Claude from being used to build or improve tools designed for surveillance." Anthropic says both changes reflect how it has enforced its previous policy. The post does not mention the Pentagon, any government contract or the designation, and nothing published in this period says what, if anything, replaces the contractual prohibitions the department refused to relax.
states.changed: The department said for the first time, through an official's statement to the BBC, that it has ceased using Anthropic products — the statement this arc's question asked for, though not a filing, and carried by one outlet only. Palantir's chief technology officer said on television that Claude is already replaced and there was no operational impact, naming no replacement for any role. The second half of the question is still open: Anthropic tightened its own weapons and surveillance prohibitions, and no document says what replaces the contract terms the department refused to relax.

questions.question: Does the department confirm completion after 30 September?
questions.would_settle: A department statement, a filing, or a second outlet obtaining the figures from the department.

settled.text: A Department of Defense official said in a statement reported by the BBC that the Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products". No filing or published department document records the completion, the statement names no replacement, and the BBC is the only outlet carrying it.

questions.question: Does Anthropic seek rehearing or Supreme Court review, and is the split with the Northern District of California resolved?
questions.would_settle: A petition for rehearing or certiorari appearing on the docket, or the mandate issuing with no petition filed.

questions.question: What replaced Claude in which Pentagon role, and what replaces the contract safeguards Anthropic refused to relax?
questions.would_settle: A department memorandum, contract action, inspector-general report or congressional testimony naming the replacement systems, or a published contract award for the replaced workloads.
